question: A 78-year-old man who underwent cardiac catheterization with revascularization of the right coronary artery 3 weeks ago and consulted for nausea and vomiting of 3 days of evolution. It presents arterial pressure of 185/85 mm Hg and purple lesions on the toes of both feet. In the analytical, urea 230 mg / dL and creatinine 5.8 mg / dL were observed. What is the most likely diagnosis?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Cardiac catheterization" -> "dislodged atherosclerotic plaques" -> "embolization to small vessels" -> "purple lesions on toes" -> "renal impairment" -> "elevated urea and creatinine" -> "Renal atheroembolic disease" -> 95%
CHAIN: "Cardiac catheterization" -> "contrast exposure" -> "renal tubular damage" -> "elevated creatinine" -> "Acute tubular necrosis by contrast" -> "nausea and vomiting" -> 70%
CHAIN: "Hypertension" -> "end-organ damage" -> "renal impairment" -> "elevated urea and creatinine" -> "Malignant arterial hypertension" -> "purple lesions" -> 60%

CHAIN: "Cardiac catheterization" -> "atherosclerotic plaque dislodgement" -> "embolization to renal arteries" -> "renal impairment" -> "elevated urea and creatinine" -> "Renal atheroembolic disease" -> 90%
CHAIN: "Hypertension" -> "renal artery stenosis" -> "reduced renal perfusion" -> "elevated creatinine" -> "Bilateral renal artery stenosis" -> "nausea and vomiting" -> 65%
analysis: The patient's symptoms and history suggest renal atheroembolic disease. The key indicators are the recent cardiac catheterization, the presence of purple lesions on the toes (livedo reticularis or 'blue toe syndrome'), and acute kidney injury with elevated creatinine and urea levels. These findings are consistent with cholesterol emboli, which can occur after vascular procedures.
